```{r ch4-geocode-coalesce-example, eval=FALSE, echo=TRUE}
    second_pass_coordinates,
    by = "property_id"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    latitude =
      coalesce(
        latitude,
        latitude_new
      ),
    longitude =
      coalesce(
        longitude,
        longitude_new
      )
  )

```

This process is important because a failed geocoding request does not
necessarily imply that the reported property is invalid. It often
reflects formatting differences between corporate disclosures and the
address representation expected by the geocoding service.

## 4.5 Final Property-Level Dataset

For reproducibility, the time-consuming web-scraping, PDF extraction and
geocoding processes are separated from the final report.

The final cleaned datasets are saved as CSV files and loaded directly
when the report is knitted.

```{r ch4-property-import}

PSPN_properties_geo <- read_csv(
  "../Data cleaning/Geo_Firms_Portfolios/DataTop3Properties/PSPN_properties_2025_final.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

SPSN_properties_geo <- read_csv(
  "../Data cleaning/Geo_Firms_Portfolios/DataTop3Properties/SPSN_properties_2025_final.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

ALLN_properties_geo <- read_csv(
  "../Data cleaning/Geo_Firms_Portfolios/DataTop3Properties/ALLN_properties_2025_final.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

```

The final property datasets contain approximately:

```{r ch4-property-count-table}

property_counts <- tibble(
  Company = c(
    "PSP Swiss Property",
    "Swiss Prime Site",
    "Allreal"
  ),

  Ticker = c(
    "PSPN",
    "SPSN",
    "ALLN"
  ),

  `Property observations` = c(
    nrow(
      PSPN_properties_geo
    ),
    nrow(
      SPSN_properties_geo
    ),
    nrow(
      ALLN_properties_geo
    )
  )
)


knitr::kable(
  property_counts,
  caption =
    "Final property-level datasets for the three largest REOCs"
)

```

The final datasets contain approximately **150 PSP observations, 122
Swiss Prime Site observations and 74 Allreal observations**.

The term *property observation* is preferable to assuming that every
reporting row necessarily corresponds to one physically separate
building. A reported property can contain several addresses or buildings
within a single investment property.

The precise variable set differs somewhat across companies because the
underlying corporate disclosures differ. However, all three datasets
contain the common geographic information required for combined spatial
analysis.

### 4.5.1 Geocoding Completeness

Before using coordinates for mapping, the final datasets are checked for
missing latitude or longitude values.

```{r ch4-geocoding-summary}

geocoding_summary <- bind_rows(

  PSPN_properties_geo |>
    summarise(
      company =
        "PSP Swiss Property",
      properties =
        n(),
      geocoded =
        sum(
          !is.na(latitude) &
          !is.na(longitude)
        )
    ),

  SPSN_properties_geo |>
    summarise(
      company =
        "Swiss Prime Site",
      properties =
        n(),
      geocoded =
        sum(
          !is.na(latitude) &
          !is.na(longitude)
        )
    ),

  ALLN_properties_geo |>
    summarise(
      company =
        "Allreal",
      properties =
        n(),
      geocoded =
        sum(
          !is.na(latitude) &
          !is.na(longitude)
        )
    )
) |>
  mutate(
    geocoding_rate =
      geocoded /
      properties
  )


knitr::kable(
  geocoding_summary |>
    mutate(
      geocoding_rate =
        scales::percent(
          geocoding_rate,
          accuracy = 0.1
        )
    ),
  col.names = c(
    "Company",
    "Property observations",
    "Geocoded observations",
    "Geocoding rate"
  ),
  caption =
    "Geocoding completeness of the final property datasets"
)

```

## 4.6 Interactive Mapping with Leaflet

The addition of latitude and longitude coordinates allows the property
portfolios to be analysed spatially.

The `leaflet` package is used because it creates an interactive map
directly within the HTML report. Unlike a static `ggplot2` figure, the
reader can:

- zoom and pan across Switzerland;
- click individual properties;
- inspect property information in popups; and
- activate or deactivate the three company portfolios separately.

The following map combines all three final datasets.

```{r ch4-map-data}

PSPN_map <- PSPN_properties_geo |>
  filter(
    !is.na(latitude),
    !is.na(longitude)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    map_address =
      coalesce(
        address,
        report_property
      ),

    popup =
      paste0(
        "<b>",
        map_address,
        "</b><br>",
        city,
        "<br><br>",
        "<b>Company:</b> ",
        company,
        "<br>",
        "<b>Property ID:</b> ",
        property_id
      )
  )


SPSN_map <- SPSN_properties_geo |>
  filter(
    !is.na(latitude),
    !is.na(longitude)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    map_address =
      coalesce(
        address,
        report_property
      ),

    popup =
      paste0(
        "<b>",
        map_address,
        "</b><br>",
        city,
        "<br><br>",
        "<b>Company:</b> ",
        company,
        "<br>",
        "<b>Property ID:</b> ",
        property_id
      )
  )


ALLN_map <- ALLN_properties_geo |>
  filter(
    !is.na(latitude),
    !is.na(longitude)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    map_address =
      coalesce(
        address,
        report_property
      ),

    popup =
      paste0(
        "<b>",
        map_address,
        "</b><br>",
        city,
        "<br><br>",
        "<b>Company:</b> ",
        company,
        "<br>",
        "<b>Property ID:</b> ",
        property_id,
        if_else(
          !is.na(property_type),
          paste0(
            "<br><b>Property type:</b> ",
            property_type
          ),
          ""
        )
      )
  )

```

```{r ch4-interactive-map, fig.width=10, fig.height=7}

leaflet() |>

  addProviderTiles(
    providers$CartoDB.Positron
  ) |>

  addCircleMarkers(
    data =
      PSPN_map,

  addCircleMarkers(
```

The map reveals the geographic footprint underlying the three largest
listed REOCs. Rather than representing an abstract financial index, the
companies consist of portfolios of physical assets concentrated in

The interactive layer control also makes it possible to compare the
geographic footprint of the three portfolios directly.

## 4.8 Methodological Limitations

The property-level dataset should be interpreted with several
limitations in mind.

First, the three companies do not disclose their portfolios using
identical definitions or variables. Consequently, not every property
characteristic is directly comparable across all three firms.

Second, a reporting row does not necessarily correspond to a single
physical building. Some observations contain multiple addresses,
adjoining buildings or larger property complexes.

Third, geocoding complex property addresses requires simplification. The
coordinates should therefore be interpreted primarily as representative
property locations rather than cadastral-level geographic precision.

Fourth, web-based information can change over time. The final CSV
datasets preserve a reproducible snapshot of the information used for
this project, while the original source URLs and report disclosures
document where the information originated.

Finally, the property-level dataset focuses on the three largest
companies and is therefore not intended to represent the full Swiss
listed real-estate universe.

## 4.9 Chapter of Choice — Conclusion

This chapter demonstrates how heterogeneous corporate disclosures can be
transformed into a structured and spatially analysable dataset.

The workflow moves through several stages:

$begin:math:display$ \\text{Corporate disclosures} \\rightarrow
\\text{data extraction} \\rightarrow \\text{cleaning and matching}
\\rightarrow \\text{address standardization} \\rightarrow
\\text{geocoding} \\rightarrow \\text{interactive mapping}.
$end:math:display$

Different source formats required different extraction techniques. PSP's
online portfolio was accessed through web scraping with `rvest`; Swiss
Prime Site's structured PDF tables were reconstructed using positional
information from `pdftools`; and Allreal's report was parsed from
extracted PDF text.

After cleaning and harmonization, property addresses were geocoded with
`tidygeocoder` and OpenStreetMap/Nominatim. The resulting coordinates
enabled the construction of an interactive `leaflet` map containing the
three largest REOC property portfolios.

The final datasets comprise approximately **150 PSP, 122 Swiss Prime
Site and 74 Allreal property observations** and connect the financial
analysis of listed companies to the physical real-estate assets
underlying them.

This workflow extends the project beyond conventional financial-data
analysis and demonstrates how web data, PDF disclosures and spatial
information can be combined within R to create a new dataset for further
empirical analysis.

# 5. Top-3 REOC Deep Dive and Conclusion

The previous chapters examined Swiss listed real-estate companies from
three perspectives: their long-run financial development, their market
performance, and their relationship with the macroeconomic environment.

This final chapter brings these perspectives together by focusing on the
three largest companies in the selected sample: **Swiss Prime Site
(SPSN), PSP Swiss Property (PSPN), and Allreal (ALLN)**.

Together, these firms represented approximately **62.9% of the selected
sample's market capitalization in 2025**. Their importance to the listed
sector therefore makes them suitable for a more detailed comparison.

The property-level dataset constructed in Chapter 4 makes it possible to
complement financial and stock-market information with characteristics
of the physical portfolios underlying the companies. The analysis
considers portfolio scale, use composition, property age, geographic
concentration, physical scale, market performance across macroeconomic
regimes, and interest-rate sensitivity.

The purpose is not to rank the companies, but to examine whether three
firms that dominate the same listed real-estate market nevertheless
represent materially different underlying exposures.

```{r ch5-setup}

TOP3_TICKERS <- c(
  "SPSN",
  "PSPN",
  "ALLN"
)

COMPANY_NAMES <- c(
  "SPSN" = "Swiss Prime Site",
  "PSPN" = "PSP Swiss Property",
  "ALLN" = "Allreal"
)

COMPANY_COLORS <- c(
  "PSP Swiss Property" = "#0072B2",
  "Swiss Prime Site"   = "#D55E00",
  "Allreal"            = "#009E73"
)

```

## 5.1 The Top 3 in Financial and Physical Context

We begin by combining selected financial and physical characteristics
into a single company profile.

The table reports the firms' 2025 market-capitalization weight within
the selected REOC sample, total assets, leverage and number of reported
property observations.

```{r ch5-top3-profile-data}

top3_market_profile <- hp_ch2 |>
  filter(
    ticker %in% TOP3_TICKERS,
    year == 2025,
    !is.na(market_cap),
    market_cap > 0
  ) |>
  group_by(ticker) |>
  slice_max(
    date,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = FALSE
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(
    ticker,
    market_cap
  ) |>
  mutate(
    sample_market_weight =
      market_cap /
      sum(
        hp_ch2 |>
          filter(
            year == 2025,
            !is.na(market_cap),
            market_cap > 0
          ) |>
          group_by(ticker) |>
          slice_max(
            date,
            n = 1,
            with_ties = FALSE
          ) |>
          ungroup() |>
          pull(market_cap)
      )
  )


top3_financial_profile <- fa |>
  filter(
    ticker %in% TOP3_TICKERS,
    year == 2025
  ) |>
  select(
    ticker,
    fa_total_assets,
    debt_to_assets
  )


top3_property_counts <- tibble(
  ticker =
    c(
      "PSPN",
      "SPSN",
      "ALLN"
    ),

  property_observations =
    c(
      nrow(
        PSPN_properties_geo
      ),
      nrow(
        SPSN_properties_geo
      ),
      nrow(
        ALLN_properties_geo
      )
    )
)


top3_profile <- top3_market_profile |>
  left_join(
    top3_financial_profile,
    by = "ticker"
  ) |>
  left_join(
    top3_property_counts,
    by = "ticker"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Company =
      recode(
        ticker,
        !!!COMPANY_NAMES
      )
  ) |>
  select(
    Company,
    sample_market_weight,
    fa_total_assets,
    debt_to_assets,
    property_observations
  ) |>
  arrange(
    desc(
      sample_market_weight
    )
  )

```

```{r ch5-top3-profile-table}

top3_profile_display <- top3_profile |>
  mutate(
    sample_market_weight =
      scales::percent(
        sample_market_weight,
        accuracy = 0.1
      ),

    fa_total_assets =
      scales::number(
        fa_total_assets,
        accuracy = 1,
        big.mark = "'"
      ),

    debt_to_assets =
      paste0(
        round(
          debt_to_assets,
          1
        ),
        "%"
      )
  )


knitr::kable(
  top3_profile_display,
  col.names = c(
    "Company",
    "2025 Market Weight",
    "Total Assets",
    "Debt / Assets",
    "Property Observations"
  ),
  caption =
    "Financial and physical profile of the three largest REOCs"
)

```

The comparison immediately illustrates an important distinction. The
three companies dominate the selected listed REOC market in financial
terms, but the number of underlying property observations differs
substantially.

PSP reports approximately 150 property observations, Swiss Prime Site
122 and Allreal 74. Property counts should not be interpreted as
measures of portfolio value because individual assets differ greatly in
size, location and use. They nevertheless provide a first indication
that similar market importance does not imply identical physical
portfolio structures.

## 5.2 Portfolio Use Composition

Property count alone says little about the economic function of the
underlying real estate. We therefore compare how reported floor or
rentable area is distributed across broad property-use categories.

Because the three companies use different reporting classifications, the
original categories are harmonized into five broad groups:

- **Office**
- **Retail**
- **Residential / Living**
- **Hospitality**
- **Other**

The harmonization is necessarily approximate. It is intended to provide
a broad comparison rather than imply perfectly identical reporting
definitions across companies.

### 5.2.1 Constructing Comparable Use Categories

For PSP Swiss Property, reported square metres are directly available
for office, retail, gastronomy and other uses.

For Swiss Prime Site, use-specific areas are estimated by multiplying
reported commercial area by the reported percentage allocated to each
use.

For Allreal's commercial properties, use-specific areas are similarly
estimated from floor space and reported use percentages. Allreal
properties classified as residential are assigned their reported
residential floor space to the residential category.

```{r ch5-use-composition-data}

psp_use <- PSPN_properties_geo |>
  summarise(
    Office =
      sum(
        office_area_m2,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    Retail =
      sum(
        retail_area_m2,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    `Residential / Living` =
      0,

    Hospitality =
      sum(
        gastronomy_area_m2,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    Other =
      sum(
        other_area_m2,
        na.rm = TRUE
      )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    company =
      "PSP Swiss Property"
  )


sps_use <- SPSN_properties_geo |>
  summarise(
    Office =
      sum(
        commercial_area_m2 *
          office_pct /
          100,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    Retail =
      sum(
        commercial_area_m2 *
          retail_pct /
          100,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    `Residential / Living` =
      sum(
        commercial_area_m2 *
          assisted_living_pct /
          100,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    Hospitality =
      sum(
        commercial_area_m2 *
          hotel_gastronomy_pct /
          100,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    Other =
      sum(
        commercial_area_m2 *
          (
            coalesce(
              storage_pct,
              0
            ) +
            coalesce(
              other_pct,
              0
            )
          ) /
          100,
        na.rm = TRUE
      )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    company =
      "Swiss Prime Site"
  )


allreal_commercial_use <- ALLN_properties_geo |>
  filter(
    property_type ==
      "Commercial"
  ) |>
  summarise(
    Office =
      sum(
        floor_space_m2 *
          office_pct /
          100,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    Retail =
      sum(
        floor_space_m2 *
          retail_pct /
          100,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    `Residential / Living` =
      sum(
        floor_space_m2 *
          residential_pct /
          100,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    Hospitality =
      0,

    Other =
      sum(
        floor_space_m2 *
          other_pct /
          100,
        na.rm = TRUE
      )
  )


allreal_residential_use <- ALLN_properties_geo |>
  filter(
    property_type ==
      "Residential"
  ) |>
  summarise(
    residential_area =
      sum(
        floor_space_m2,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    additional_other_area =
      sum(
        other_uses_m2,
        na.rm = TRUE
      )
  )


allreal_use <- allreal_commercial_use |>
  mutate(
    `Residential / Living` =
      `Residential / Living` +
      allreal_residential_use$residential_area,

    Other =
      Other +
      allreal_residential_use$additional_other_area,

    company =
      "Allreal"
  )


use_composition <- bind_rows(
  psp_use,
  sps_use,
  allreal_use
) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -company,
    names_to =
      "use_type",
    values_to =
      "area_m2"
  ) |>
  filter(
    is.finite(
      area_m2
    ),
    area_m2 >= 0
  ) |>
  group_by(company) |>
  mutate(
    total_classified_area =
      sum(
        area_m2,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    share =
      area_m2 /
      total_classified_area
  ) |>
  ungroup()

```

### 5.2.2 Portfolio Use Mix

```{r ch5-use-composition-plot, fig.width=10, fig.height=5.5}

ggplot(
  use_composition,
  aes(
    x = company,
    y = share,
    fill = use_type
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    width = 0.65
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels =
      scales::percent,
    limits =
      c(
        0,
        1
      ),
    expand =
      expansion(
        mult =
          c(
            0,
            0
          )
      )
  ) +
  labs(
    title =
      "Use Composition of the Top-3 Property Portfolios",
    subtitle =
      "Share of classified rentable, commercial or floor area",
    x =
      NULL,
    y =
      "Share of classified area",
    fill =
      "Property use"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position =
      "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor =
      element_blank()
  )

```

The 100% stacked bars reveal differences in the economic composition of
the portfolios that are not visible from company size alone.

The chart should be interpreted as a comparison of **reported and
harmonized area categories**, rather than as a perfectly standardized
property classification. Nevertheless, it illustrates that the three
listed firms provide different combinations of office, retail,
residential and other real-estate exposure.

This is important from an investor perspective because property-use
composition can influence rental-income stability, tenant structure and
exposure to different parts of the economic cycle.

## 5.3 Portfolio Age

The age distribution of the portfolios provides a second dimension along
which the three companies differ.

Construction years are extracted from each company's property-level
data. Where a disclosure contains more than one construction year, the
first reported four-digit year is used as a simplified reference point.

```{r ch5-construction-data}

construction_data <- bind_rows(

  PSPN_properties_geo |>
    transmute(
      company =
        "PSP Swiss Property",

      property_id,

      construction_year =
        str_extract(
          as.character(
            year_construction
          ),
          "\\d{4}"
        ) |>
        as.numeric()
    ),

  SPSN_properties_geo |>
    transmute(
      company =
        "Swiss Prime Site",

      property_id,

      construction_year =
        str_extract(
          as.character(
            year_construction
          ),
          "\\d{4}"
        ) |>
        as.numeric()
    ),

  ALLN_properties_geo |>
    transmute(
      company =
        "Allreal",

      property_id,

      construction_year =
        str_extract(
          as.character(
            year_construction
          ),
          "\\d{4}"
        ) |>
        as.numeric()
    )
) |>
  filter(
    !is.na(
      construction_year
    ),
    construction_year >= 1600,
    construction_year <= 2025
  )

```

```{r ch5-construction-histogram, fig.width=10, fig.height=7}

ggplot(
  construction_data,
  aes(
    x =
      construction_year,
    fill =
      company
  )
) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth =
      10,
    boundary =
      1900
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ company,
    ncol =
      1
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values =
      COMPANY_COLORS
  ) +
  labs(
    title =
      "Distribution of Property Construction Years",
    subtitle =
      "Construction years grouped into ten-year intervals",
    x =
      "Year of construction",
    y =
      "Number of property observations"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position =
      "none",
    panel.grid.minor =
      element_blank()
  )

```

The distributions demonstrate that portfolio age is not uniform across
the three firms.

Rather than relying only on an average construction year, the histogram
shows both the central concentration and the historical tails of each
portfolio. PSP in particular contains properties spanning a broad range
of construction periods, while the Allreal dataset is more concentrated
in comparatively recent construction periods.

These differences may reflect distinct acquisition histories,
redevelopment strategies and geographic specializations.

## 5.4 Geographic Concentration

The property-level dataset also allows the geographic concentration of
the three portfolios to be compared directly.

City names are first harmonized so that alternative language versions
such as Zürich and Zurich or Genève and Geneva are treated as the same
location.

```{r ch5-city-data}

city_data <- bind_rows(

  PSPN_properties_geo |>
    transmute(
      company =
        "PSP Swiss Property",
      property_id,
      city
    ),

  SPSN_properties_geo |>
    transmute(
      company =
        "Swiss Prime Site",
      property_id,
      city
    ),

  ALLN_properties_geo |>
    transmute(
      company =
        "Allreal",
      property_id,
      city
    )
) |>
  mutate(
    city = case_when(

      city %in%
        c(
          "Zurich",
          "Zürich"
        ) ~
        "Zurich",

      city %in%
        c(
          "Geneva",
          "Genève",
          "Genf"
        ) ~
        "Geneva",

      city %in%
        c(
          "Bern",
          "Berne"
        ) ~
        "Bern",

      TRUE ~
        city
    )
  ) |>
  filter(
    !is.na(
      city
    ),
    city != ""
  )


city_counts <- city_data |>
  count(
    city,
    company,
    name =
      "properties"
  ) |>
  group_by(city) |>
  mutate(
    total_properties =
      sum(
        properties
      )
  ) |>
  ungroup()


top_cities <- city_counts |>
  distinct(
    city,
    total_properties
  ) |>
  slice_max(
    total_properties,
    n = 10,
    with_ties = FALSE
  ) |>
  pull(city)

```

```{r ch5-city-plot, fig.width=10, fig.height=6}

city_counts |>
  filter(
    city %in%
      top_cities
  ) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x =
        reorder(
          city,
          total_properties
        ),
      y =
        properties,
      fill =
        company
    )
  ) +
  geom_col(
    position =
      "dodge"
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values =
      COMPANY_COLORS
  ) +
  labs(
    title =
      "Geographic Concentration of the Top-3 Portfolios",
    subtitle =
      "Top 10 cities by number of reported properties",
    x =
      NULL,
    y =
      "Number of property observations",
    fill =
      "Portfolio"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position =
      "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor =
      element_blank()
  )

```

The firms have materially different geographic footprints. PSP has
particularly substantial exposure to Zurich, while the relative
importance of Basel, Geneva, Lausanne and other locations differs across
the three portfolios.

The interactive map in **Chapter 4.6** provides the complementary
spatial view and allows individual property locations to be inspected
directly.

Together, the city comparison and interactive map indicate that
concentration in the same listed market does not translate into
identical geographic real-estate exposure.

## 5.5 Physical Scale and Development Intensity

Portfolio composition and location can be complemented by the physical
scale of individual properties.

For this comparison, the reported site or land area is plotted against
the corresponding rentable, commercial or floor area.

The source terminology differs across firms:

- PSP reports land area and rentable area;
- Swiss Prime Site reports site area and commercial area;
- Allreal reports site area and floor space.

The variables are therefore treated as approximately comparable
indicators of **land footprint** and **usable property area**, rather
than as perfectly identical accounting definitions.

```{r ch5-property-area-data}

property_area_scatter <- bind_rows(

  PSPN_properties_geo |>
    transmute(
      company =
        "PSP Swiss Property",

      property_id,

      site_area_m2 =
        land_area_m2,

      property_area_m2 =
        rentable_area_m2
    ),

  SPSN_properties_geo |>
    transmute(
      company =
        "Swiss Prime Site",

      property_id,

      site_area_m2 =
        site_area_m2,

      property_area_m2 =
        commercial_area_m2
    ),

  ALLN_properties_geo |>
    transmute(
      company =
        "Allreal",

      property_id,

      site_area_m2 =
        site_area_m2,

      property_area_m2 =
        floor_space_m2
    )
) |>
  filter(
    !is.na(
      site_area_m2
    ),
    !is.na(
      property_area_m2
    ),
    site_area_m2 > 0,
    property_area_m2 > 0
  )

```

```{r ch5-property-area-plot, fig.width=10, fig.height=6}

ggplot(
  property_area_scatter,
  aes(
    x =
      site_area_m2,
    y =
      property_area_m2,
    color =
      company
  )
) +
  geom_abline(
    slope =
      1,
    intercept =
      0,
    linetype =
      "dashed",
    linewidth =
      0.6
  ) +
  geom_point(
    alpha =

      2.4
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values =
      COMPANY_COLORS
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(
    labels =
      scales::label_number(
        big.mark = "'"
      )
  ) +
  scale_y_log10(
    labels =
      scales::label_number(
        big.mark = "'"
      )
  ) +
  labs(
    title =
      "Land Footprint and Usable Property Area",
    subtitle =

    x =

```

The diagonal reference line represents properties for which reported
usable area equals the reported site or land area.

Observations above the line have more reported usable floor area than
land area, which can be consistent with more intensive or multi-storey
development. Observations below the line have a larger land footprint
relative to their reported usable area.

Because the underlying companies use different reporting definitions,
the figure should be interpreted as a broad physical comparison rather
than a precise measure of development density. Even with this
limitation, the dispersion illustrates substantial heterogeneity in the
scale and physical structure of individual assets.

## 5.6 Top-3 Performance Across Macroeconomic Regimes

The physical portfolios differ, but the three firms also operate in the
same financial and macroeconomic environment.

Chapter 3 showed that aggregate REOC returns vary across monetary
regimes and that changes in long-term Swiss government yields are
particularly relevant for listed real-estate returns.

We therefore return to the five macroeconomic regimes defined in Chapter
3 and compare the **average monthly return of each Top-3 firm** within
each period.

```{r ch5-regime-performance-data}

top3_regime_returns <- hp_ch2 |>
  filter(
    ticker %in%
      TOP3_TICKERS,
    !is.na(
      monthly_return
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    month =
      floor_date(
        date,
        "month"
      ),

    regime =
      case_when(

        month <
          as.Date(
            "2008-09-01"
          ) ~
          "Pre-GFC",

        month >=
          as.Date(
            "2008-09-01"
          ) &
          month <
          as.Date(
            "2015-01-01"
          ) ~
          "Post-GFC Low Rates",

        month >=
          as.Date(
            "2015-01-01"
          ) &
          month <
          as.Date(
            "2022-06-01"
          ) ~
          "Negative-Rate Era",

        month >=
          as.Date(
            "2022-06-01"
          ) &
          month <
          as.Date(
            "2024-01-01"
          ) ~
          "Hiking Cycle",

        month >=
          as.Date(
            "2024-01-01"
          ) &
          month <=
          as.Date(
            "2025-12-31"
          ) ~
          "Post-Hiking / Cuts",

        TRUE ~
          NA_character_
      )
  ) |>
  filter(
    !is.na(
      regime
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(
    ticker,
    regime
  ) |>
  summarise(
    mean_monthly_return =
      mean(
        monthly_return,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    median_monthly_return =
      median(
        monthly_return,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    n_months =
      n(),

    .groups =
      "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    company =
      recode(
        ticker,
        !!!COMPANY_NAMES
      ),

    regime =
      factor(
        regime,
        levels =
          c(
            "Pre-GFC",
            "Post-GFC Low Rates",
            "Negative-Rate Era",
            "Hiking Cycle",
            "Post-Hiking / Cuts"
          )
      )
  )

```

```{r ch5-regime-heatmap, fig.width=10, fig.height=5.5}

ggplot(
  top3_regime_returns,
  aes(
    x =
      regime,
    y =
      company,
    fill =
      mean_monthly_return
  )
) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      label =
        scales::percent(
          mean_monthly_return,
          accuracy = 0.1
        )
    ),
    size =
      4
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    midpoint =
      0,
    labels =
      scales::percent
  ) +
  labs(
    title =
      "Top-3 REOC Performance Across Macroeconomic Regimes",
    subtitle =
      "Average monthly return within each regime",
    x =
      NULL,
    y =
      NULL,
    fill =
      "Average\nmonthly return"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid =
      element_blank(),
    axis.text.x =
      element_text(
        angle =
          20,
        hjust =
          1
      )
  )

```

The heatmap allows the same macroeconomic environments to be compared
across firms without reducing each company's experience to one
full-sample return measure.

Differences across rows indicate that companies exposed to the same
Swiss interest-rate environment did not necessarily generate identical
market outcomes. This is consistent with the firm-level heterogeneity
identified in Chapter 3.

The comparison is descriptive: the regime averages combine many
influences beyond monetary policy, including market-wide shocks, changes
in portfolio composition and company-specific developments.

## 5.7 Interest-Rate Sensitivity of the Top 3

The regime analysis can be complemented by a more direct measure of
interest-rate sensitivity.

Chapter 3 examined monthly stock returns against changes in the 10-year
Swiss Confederation yield. Here, the same relationship is estimated only
for the three dominant companies.

Inflation is retained as an additional control to make the estimates
consistent with the firm-level specification used in Chapter 3.

```{r ch5-top3-rate-sensitivity}

top3_firm_macro <- hp_macro |>
  mutate(
    date =
      as.Date(
        date
      ),

    month =
      floor_date(
        date,
        "month"
      )
  ) |>
  filter(
    ticker %in%
      TOP3_TICKERS,
    month <=
      as.Date(
        "2025-12-31"
      )
  ) |>
  select(
    ticker,
    month,
    monthly_return
  ) |>
  left_join(
    macro_monthly |>
      select(
        month,
        d_long_rate,
        inflation
      ),
    by =
      "month"
  )


top3_return_sensitivity <- top3_firm_macro |>
  filter(
    complete.cases(
      monthly_return,
      d_long_rate,
      inflation
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(
    ticker
  ) |>
  nest() |>
  mutate(
    model =
      map(
        data,
        ~ lm(
          monthly_return ~
            d_long_rate +
            inflation,
          data =
            .x
        )
      ),

    tidy_model =
      map(
        model,
        broom::tidy
      )
  ) |>
  select(
    ticker,
    tidy_model
  ) |>
  unnest(
    tidy_model
  ) |>
  filter(
    term ==
      "d_long_rate"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    lower =
      estimate -
      1.96 *
      std.error,

    upper =
      estimate +
      1.96 *
      std.error,

    company =
      recode(
        ticker,
        !!!COMPANY_NAMES
      )
  )

```

```{r ch5-top3-rate-sensitivity-plot, fig.width=9, fig.height=5}

ggplot(
  top3_return_sensitivity,
  aes(
    x =
      estimate,
    y =
      reorder(
        company,
        estimate
      )
  )
) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept =
      0,
    linetype =
      "dashed",
    linewidth =
      0.5
  ) +
  geom_errorbarh(
    aes(
      xmin =
        lower,
      xmax =
        upper
    ),
    height =
      0.15
  ) +
  geom_point(
    size =
      3
  ) +
  labs(
    title =
      "Top-3 Market Sensitivity to Long-Term Interest Rates",
    subtitle =
      "Monthly-return coefficient on changes in the 10-year Confederation yield",
    x =
      "Estimated return sensitivity",
    y =
      NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor =
      element_blank()
  )

```

The estimates make the distinction between **sector exposure** and
**company-specific exposure** explicit. All three companies operate
within the same listed real-estate market, but the magnitude of the
historical relationship between their returns and changes in long-term
yields is not identical.

The confidence intervals also provide an indication of estimation
uncertainty rather than presenting the individual coefficients as exact
sensitivities.

### 5.7.1 Interest Rates and Financial Structure

The market-response analysis can be compared with the leverage
relationships identified in RQ3.

```{r ch5-top3-yield-leverage}

top3_yield_leverage <- fa_rq3 |>
  filter(
    ticker %in%
      TOP3_TICKERS
  ) |>
  group_by(
    ticker
  ) |>
  summarise(
    observations =
      sum(
        complete.cases(
          confederation_10y,
          debt_to_assets
        )
      ),

    yield_leverage_correlation =
      cor(
        confederation_10y,
        debt_to_assets,
        use =
          "complete.obs"
      ),

    .groups =
      "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Company =
      recode(
        ticker,
        !!!COMPANY_NAMES
      ),

    `Yield–Leverage Correlation` =
      round(
        yield_leverage_correlation,
        2
      )
  ) |>
  select(
    Company,
    Observations =
      observations,
    `Yield–Leverage Correlation`
  )


knitr::kable(
  top3_yield_leverage,
  caption =
    "Firm-specific relationship between long-term government yields and leverage"
)

```

This comparison reinforces the broader finding from Chapter 3: the same
macroeconomic variable can be associated differently with different
companies.

Swiss Prime Site and PSP Swiss Property display relatively strong
positive historical relationships between long-term yields and leverage,
whereas Allreal's relationship is substantially weaker.

The combination of market-return and balance-sheet evidence therefore
argues against treating the Top-3 firms as interchangeable exposures.

## 5.8 Bringing Financial and Physical Portfolios Together

The Top-3 analysis brings together the main strands of the report.

At the **market level**, Swiss Prime Site, PSP Swiss Property and
Allreal account for a substantial majority of the market capitalization
of the selected listed REOC sample.

At the **property level**, however, their portfolios differ along
several dimensions:

- the number of reported properties;
- geographic concentration;
- property-use composition;
- construction-year distribution; and
- the relationship between land footprint and usable property area.

At the **financial level**, the firms also differ in leverage and in the
historical relationship between their balance sheets and long-term
government yields.

Finally, at the **equity-market level**, their returns do not behave
identically across macroeconomic regimes or exhibit exactly the same
estimated sensitivity to long-term interest-rate changes.

The combined evidence therefore suggests that **market concentration
does not imply portfolio homogeneity**.

A listed Swiss REOC index may appear to represent a single sector, but
much of its market value is concentrated in a small number of companies
with materially different physical portfolios and company-specific
financial characteristics.

This heterogeneity is economically important. Exposure to office, retail
or residential assets, concentration in particular cities, property age
and physical intensity may influence how an individual company reacts to
changes in occupier demand, financing costs and capital-market
conditions.

The present analysis does not establish that any one physical portfolio
characteristic causes a particular stock-market response. Rather, it
demonstrates why aggregate sector relationships should be interpreted
alongside the composition of the firms underlying them.

## 5.9 Overall Conclusion

This report examined Swiss listed real-estate operating companies
through a combination of financial, market, macroeconomic and
property-level data.

**RQ1** asked how the financial characteristics and market performance
of Swiss listed REOCs developed over time. The results showed a sector
dominated by a relatively small number of large companies, with Swiss
Prime Site, PSP Swiss Property and Allreal accounting for approximately
62.9% of the selected sample's market capitalization in 2025. The sector
nevertheless contains meaningful differences in firm size, leverage and
market performance.

**RQ2** examined how stock-market performance is associated with changes
in the macroeconomic environment. The clearest relationship appears for
long-term interest rates: increases in the 10-year Swiss Confederation
yield tend to coincide with weaker monthly REOC returns. However,
performance differs across monetary regimes and the estimated degree of
interest-rate sensitivity varies across firms.

**RQ3** examined the relationship between macroeconomic conditions and
firm fundamentals. A positive pooled association exists between
long-term government yields and leverage, but this relationship becomes
substantially weaker when annual changes and persistent firm-specific
differences are considered. This suggests that the pooled association
partly reflects longer-term and cross-firm patterns rather than a
uniform short-run leverage response.

The **Chapter of Choice** extended the project from standardized
financial datasets to the physical portfolios underlying the companies.
Corporate webpages and PDF disclosures were transformed into a geocoded
property-level dataset using web scraping, PDF extraction, text
cleaning, address matching and geocoding. The resulting interactive map
provides a spatial representation of the assets underlying the three
dominant listed REOCs.

The final Top-3 comparison demonstrates why these perspectives are
complementary. The three firms dominate the same listed sector but
differ in property count, use composition, geographic concentration,
property age, physical characteristics, financial structure and
historical macroeconomic sensitivity.

The central conclusion of the report is therefore that the Swiss listed
real-estate market is **concentrated but heterogeneous**.

Macroeconomic conditions, particularly interest rates, are relevant for
listed real-estate performance, but their effects are not uniform across
companies. Understanding the sector therefore requires looking beyond
aggregate indices and considering both the financial characteristics of
individual firms and the physical property portfolios that ultimately
underpin them.

## 5.10 Limitations and Further Research

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the results.

First, the selected sample deliberately focuses on economically
significant listed REOCs and therefore does not represent every listed
Swiss real-estate company equally.

Second, both the monthly and annual datasets form unbalanced panels
because companies enter the available historical data at different
dates.

Third, the statistical analyses are primarily descriptive and
associational. Correlations, regime comparisons and regressions do not
establish causal effects of macroeconomic variables on company
performance or financial policy.

Fourth, the number of independent macroeconomic time periods is
considerably smaller than the number of firm-level observations because
the same Swiss macroeconomic conditions apply to all firms in a given
month or year.

Fifth, the property-level dataset combines corporate disclosures that
differ in structure and definitions. Variables such as rentable area,
commercial area and floor space are economically related but are not
necessarily defined identically by each company.

Finally, the property-level deep dive covers only the three dominant
firms and largely represents a 2025 snapshot. A particularly valuable
extension would be to construct comparable historical property
portfolios for all three companies. If consistent acquisition, disposal
and redevelopment histories became available, future research could
examine whether changes in physical portfolio composition are associated
with subsequent changes in financial performance and macroeconomic
sensitivity.

### A.2 Rolling Correlations with Market Benchmarks

The main analysis reports full-sample return correlations. As an
additional robustness check, the following figure shows how the
correlation between the constructed REOC portfolios and the Swiss market
benchmarks varies over time.

A 36-month rolling window is used.

```{r appendix-rolling-correlations, fig.width=10, fig.height=6}

library(slider)

rolling_correlations <-
  portfolio_benchmarks |>
  filter(
    month >= analysis_start,
    month <= analysis_end
  ) |>
  arrange(month) |>
  mutate(

    EW_REAL =
      slide2_dbl(
        ew_return,
        real_return,
        ~ cor(
          .x,
          .y,
          use = "complete.obs"
        ),
        .before = 35,
        .complete = TRUE
      ),

    VW_REAL =
      slide2_dbl(
        vw_return,
        real_return,
        ~ cor(
          .x,
          .y,
          use = "complete.obs"
        ),
        .before = 35,
        .complete = TRUE
      ),

    EW_SPI =
      slide2_dbl(
        ew_return,
        spi_return,
        ~ cor(
          .x,
          .y,
          use = "complete.obs"
        ),
        .before = 35,
        .complete = TRUE
      ),

    VW_SPI =
      slide2_dbl(
        vw_return,
        spi_return,
        ~ cor(
          .x,
          .y,
          use = "complete.obs"
        ),
        .before = 35,
        .complete = TRUE
      )
  )

rolling_corr_long <-
  rolling_correlations |>
  select(
    month,
    EW_REAL,
    VW_REAL,
    EW_SPI,
    VW_SPI
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -month,
    names_to = "series",
    values_to = "correlation"
  )

ggplot(
  rolling_corr_long,
  aes(
    x = month,
    y = correlation,
    color = series
  )
) +
  geom_line(
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Rolling Correlation with Swiss Market Benchmarks",
    subtitle = "36-month rolling correlations of EW and VW portfolio returns",
    x = NULL,
    y = "36-month correlation",
    color = "Series"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

```

The rolling correlations show that benchmark relationships are not
constant through time. The portfolios generally remain more closely
related to the listed real-estate benchmark than to the broader equity
market, while periods of market stress and structural change produce
substantial variation in correlation

## B. Additional Analysis for RQ2

This section contains supplementary analyses supporting the
investigation of the relationship between REOC market performance and
the Swiss macroeconomic environment.

The main report focuses on the most economically relevant results. The
additional tables and figures below document data coverage, alternative
macroeconomic relationships, volatility, and more detailed regression
results.

### B.1 Monthly Macroeconomic Data Coverage

The monthly macroeconomic dataset is structured as a firm-month panel.
Because macroeconomic variables are common to all firms observed in a
given month, the data are reduced to one observation per month before
evaluating macroeconomic coverage.

```{r appendix-rq2-macro-coverage}

macro_coverage_data <- hp_macro |>
  mutate(
    date = as.Date(date),
    month = floor_date(date, "month")
  ) |>
  distinct(
    month,
    .keep_all = TRUE
  ) |>
  arrange(month)

macro_variables_coverage <- c(
  "libor_3m_chf",
  "snb_policy_rate",
  "confederation_10y",
  "sfso_inflation_according_to_the_national_consumer_price_index",
  "snb_core_inflation_trimmed_mean1",
  "jobless_rate_sa",
  "apartments_wuest_transaction",
  "houses_wuest_transaction",
  "gdp"
)

monthly_macro_missingness <- macro_coverage_data |>
  summarise(
    across(
      all_of(macro_variables_coverage),
      ~ mean(is.na(.))
    )
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "missing_share"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    available_share =
      1 - missing_share,

    variable = recode(
      variable,
      libor_3m_chf =
        "3M CHF LIBOR",
      snb_policy_rate =
        "SNB policy rate",
      confederation_10y =
        "10Y Confederation yield",
      sfso_inflation_according_to_the_national_consumer_price_index =
        "Headline inflation",
      snb_core_inflation_trimmed_mean1 =
        "Core inflation",
      jobless_rate_sa =
        "Seasonally adjusted unemployment",
      apartments_wuest_transaction =
        "Apartment transaction-price index",
      houses_wuest_transaction =
        "House transaction-price index",
      gdp =
        "GDP"
    ),

    missing_share =
      scales::percent(
        missing_share,
        accuracy = 0.1
      ),

    available_share =
      scales::percent(
        available_share,
        accuracy = 0.1
      )
  )


knitr::kable(
  monthly_macro_missingness,
  col.names = c(
    "Macroeconomic variable",
    "Missing observations",
    "Available observations"
  ),
  caption =
    "Availability of selected monthly macroeconomic variables"
)

```

The coverage differs substantially across variables. Inflation and
labour-market series provide relatively broad coverage, while some
interest-rate measures apply only to particular monetary-policy periods.
GDP and selected alternative property-price series are substantially
sparser and are therefore treated primarily as secondary or contextual
variables.

### B.2 Construction of the Continuous Short-Term Interest Rate

The sample spans a change in the Swiss monetary-policy framework. The
3-month CHF LIBOR provides the short-term interest-rate indicator during
the earlier part of the sample, while the SNB policy rate becomes
available around the 2019 framework transition.

The following table documents the splice around that transition.

```{r appendix-short-rate-splice}

short_rate_splice <- macro_coverage_data |>
  mutate(
    short_rate =
      coalesce(
        libor_3m_chf,
        snb_policy_rate
      )
  ) |>
  filter(
    month >=
      as.Date("2019-01-01"),
    month <=
      as.Date("2019-12-01")
  ) |>
  select(
    month,
    libor_3m_chf,
    snb_policy_rate,
    short_rate
  )


knitr::kable(
  short_rate_splice,
  digits = 3,
  col.names = c(
    "Month",
    "3M CHF LIBOR",
    "SNB policy rate",
    "Constructed short rate"
  ),
  caption =
    "Short-term interest-rate splice around the 2019 monetary-policy framework transition"
)

```

The constructed series uses the available LIBOR observation during the
earlier period and the SNB policy rate thereafter. This creates a
continuous indicator suitable for the long historical analysis while
acknowledging that the underlying monetary-policy reference changed over
time.

### B.3 Full RQ2 Multivariable Regression Results

The main chapter presents a compact regression specification using
changes in short- and long-term interest rates, inflation and changes in
unemployment.

As an additional robustness analysis, the earlier exploratory
specification also includes monthly growth in apartment transaction
prices.

```{r appendix-rq2-full-regression-data}

portfolio_macro_appendix <- portfolio_macro |>
  arrange(month) |>
  mutate(
    apartments_growth =
      apartments_wuest_transaction /
      lag(apartments_wuest_transaction) -
      1,

    houses_growth =
      houses_wuest_transaction /
      lag(houses_wuest_transaction) -
      1
  )

```

```{r appendix-rq2-full-regression}

pooled_ew_full <- lm(
  ew_return ~
    d_short_rate +
    d_long_rate +
    inflation +
    d_jobless_rate +
    apartments_growth,
  data = portfolio_macro_appendix
)


pooled_vw_full <- lm(
  vw_return ~
    d_short_rate +
    d_long_rate +
    inflation +
    d_jobless_rate +
    apartments_growth,
  data = portfolio_macro_appendix
)


rq2_full_regression_table <- bind_rows(
  broom::tidy(
    pooled_ew_full
  ) |>
    mutate(
      Portfolio =
        "Equal Weighted"
    ),

  broom::tidy(
    pooled_vw_full
  ) |>
    mutate(
      Portfolio =
        "Value Weighted"
    )
) |>
  mutate(
    term = recode(
      term,
      `(Intercept)` =
        "Intercept",
      d_short_rate =
        "Change in short-term rate",
      d_long_rate =
        "Change in 10-year yield",
      inflation =
        "Inflation",
      d_jobless_rate =
        "Change in unemployment",
      apartments_growth =
        "Apartment-price growth"
    )
  ) |>
  select(
    Portfolio,
    term,
    estimate,
    std.error,
    statistic,
    p.value
  ) |>
  mutate(
    across(
      where(is.numeric),
      ~ round(.x, 4)
    )
  )


knitr::kable(
  rq2_full_regression_table,
  col.names = c(
    "Portfolio",
    "Variable",
    "Estimate",
    "Std. error",
    "t-statistic",
    "p-value"
  ),
  caption =
    "Extended portfolio-level regression results for RQ2"
)

```

The extended specification should be interpreted as a robustness and
exploratory exercise rather than as a causal model. The inclusion of
several contemporaneous macroeconomic variables may introduce
correlation among explanatory variables, and the estimated coefficients
should therefore be interpreted cautiously.

### B.4 Inflation and REOC Returns

Inflation is examined separately as an additional macroeconomic
indicator. The original exploratory analysis found relatively weak
full-sample correlations between inflation and both aggregate REOC
portfolios.

```{r appendix-inflation-returns, fig.width=10, fig.height=5.5}

inflation_return_data <- portfolio_macro |>
  select(
    month,
    inflation,
    ew_return,
    vw_return
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(
      ew_return,
      vw_return
    ),
    names_to = "portfolio_type",
    values_to = "return"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    portfolio_type = recode(
      portfolio_type,
      ew_return =
        "Equal Weighted",
      vw_return =
        "Value Weighted"
    )
  )


ggplot(
  inflation_return_data |>
    filter(
      is.finite(inflation),
      is.finite(return)
    ),
  aes(
    x = inflation,
    y = return
  )
) +
  geom_point(
    alpha = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = TRUE
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ portfolio_type
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels =
      scales::percent
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Inflation and REOC Portfolio Returns",
    subtitle = "Monthly observations",
    x = "Inflation (%)",
    y = "Monthly portfolio return"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor =
      element_blank()
  )

```

The scatterplots show substantial dispersion around the fitted
relationships. Inflation alone therefore explains relatively little of
the month-to-month variation in REOC returns.

### B.5 Labour-Market Conditions and REOC Returns

Changes in seasonally adjusted unemployment provide an additional
measure of changes in the economic environment.

```{r appendix-unemployment-returns, fig.width=10, fig.height=5.5}

unemployment_return_data <- portfolio_macro |>
  select(
    month,
    d_jobless_rate,
    ew_return,
    vw_return
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(
      ew_return,
      vw_return
    ),
    names_to = "portfolio_type",
    values_to = "return"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    portfolio_type = recode(
      portfolio_type,
      ew_return =
        "Equal Weighted",
      vw_return =
        "Value Weighted"
    )
  )


ggplot(
  unemployment_return_data |>
    filter(
      is.finite(d_jobless_rate),
      is.finite(return)
    ),
  aes(
    x = d_jobless_rate,
    y = return
  )
) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_point(
    alpha = 0.4
  ) +

  ) +

  ) +

  ) +

```

As with inflation, the large dispersion of monthly observations
indicates that changes in unemployment are not a dominant standalone

### B.6 Property-Market Momentum and REOC Returns

Because listed REOCs hold direct real-estate assets, an additional
exploratory analysis compares listed market returns with changes in
Swiss residential transaction-price indices.

The apartment and house price indices are converted into month-to-month
growth rates.

```{r appendix-property-price-returns, fig.width=10, fig.height=6}

property_return_data <- portfolio_macro_appendix |>
  select(
    month,
    vw_return,
    apartments_growth,
    houses_growth
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(
      apartments_growth,
      houses_growth
    ),
    names_to = "property_measure",
    values_to = "property_growth"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    property_measure = recode(
      property_measure,
      apartments_growth =
        "Apartment Prices",
      houses_growth =
        "House Prices"
    )
  )


ggplot(
  property_return_data |>
    filter(
      is.finite(property_growth),
      is.finite(vw_return)
    ),
  aes(
    x = property_growth,
    y = vw_return
  )
) +
  geom_point(
    alpha = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = TRUE
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ property_measure,
    scales = "free_x"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels =
      scales::percent
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels =
      scales::percent
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Property-Price Momentum and REOC Market Returns",
    subtitle = "Residential transaction-price growth versus VW portfolio return",
    x = "Monthly property-price growth",

  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor =

  )

```

These comparisons are exploratory. Direct property markets and listed
securities operate at different frequencies and may incorporate
information at different speeds, so a weak contemporaneous monthly
relationship does not imply that underlying property-market conditions
are irrelevant to REOC values.

### B.7 Rolling REOC Portfolio Volatility

The main report focuses on return levels and macroeconomic associations.
As an additional market-risk measure, the following figure presents
rolling realised volatility.

A 12-month rolling standard deviation of monthly returns is used.

```{r appendix-rq2-rolling-volatility, fig.width=10, fig.height=6}

rolling_volatility <- portfolio_macro |>
  arrange(month) |>
  mutate(
    ew_vol_12m =
      slider::slide_dbl(
        ew_return,
        sd,
        .before = 11,
        .complete = TRUE
      ),

    vw_vol_12m =
      slider::slide_dbl(
        vw_return,
        sd,
        .before = 11,
        .complete = TRUE
      )
  ) |>
  select(
    month,
    ew_vol_12m,
    vw_vol_12m
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(
      ew_vol_12m,
      vw_vol_12m
    ),
    names_to = "portfolio_type",
    values_to = "volatility"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    portfolio_type = recode(
      portfolio_type,
      ew_vol_12m =
        "Equal Weighted",
      vw_vol_12m =
        "Value Weighted"
    )
  )


ggplot(
  rolling_volatility,
  aes(
    x = month,
    y = volatility,
    color = portfolio_type
  )
) +
  geom_line(
    linewidth = 0.8,
    na.rm = TRUE
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels =
      scales::percent
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Rolling Volatility of REOC Portfolio Returns",
    subtitle = "12-month rolling standard deviation of monthly returns",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Rolling monthly volatility",
    color = "Portfolio"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position =
      "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor =
      element_blank()
  )

```

The rolling measure shows that REOC return volatility varies
considerably over time. Periods of heightened market uncertainty
therefore affect not only realised returns but also the dispersion of
monthly performance.

### B.8 Full Firm-Level RQ2 Sensitivity Estimates

Section 3.1.4 visualises firm-specific sensitivity to changes in
long-term interest rates. The complete regression estimates are reported
below.

Each firm-level regression takes the form

$begin:math:display$ R\_{i,t} = \\alpha_i + \\beta\_{1,i}\\Delta
Yield_t + \\beta\_{2,i}Inflation_t + \\varepsilon\_{i,t}.
$end:math:display$

```{r appendix-rq2-firm-sensitivity-table}

firm_sensitivity_full <- firm_macro |>
  filter(
    !is.na(monthly_return)
  ) |>
  group_by(ticker) |>
  filter(
    n() >= 24
  ) |>
  nest() |>
  mutate(
    model =
      map(
        data,
        ~ lm(
          monthly_return ~
            d_long_rate +
            inflation,
          data = .x
        )
      ),

    tidy_model =
      map(
        model,
        broom::tidy
      )
  ) |>
  select(
    ticker,
    tidy_model
  ) |>
  unnest(
    tidy_model
  ) |>
  filter(
    term %in%
      c(
        "d_long_rate",
        "inflation"
      )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    term = recode(
      term,
      d_long_rate =
        "Change in 10-year yield",
      inflation =
        "Inflation"
    )
  ) |>
  select(
    ticker,
    term,
    estimate,
    std.error,
    statistic,
    p.value
  ) |>
  arrange(
    term,
    estimate
  ) |>
  mutate(
    across(
      where(is.numeric),
      ~ round(.x, 4)
    )
  )


knitr::kable(
  firm_sensitivity_full,
  col.names = c(
    "Ticker",
    "Variable",
    "Estimate",
    "Std. error",
    "t-statistic",
    "p-value"
  ),
  caption =
    "Firm-level RQ2 regression estimates"
)

```

The detailed estimates reinforce the main finding that REOCs differ in
the magnitude of their exposure to macroeconomic conditions. These
coefficients remain descriptive associations rather than causal
estimates.

## C. Additional Analysis for RQ3

This section reports additional descriptive and statistical results
concerning the relationship between firm fundamentals and the
macroeconomic environment.

The main report focuses on the long-term yield–leverage relationship and
the contrast between pooled and within-firm evidence. The following
material documents the broader exploratory analysis supporting that
choice.

### C.1 Annual Firm-Level Data Coverage

The annual accounting panel is unbalanced because the number of
historical observations differs across firms.

```{r appendix-rq3-firm-coverage}

annual_firm_coverage <- fa_rq3 |>
  group_by(ticker) |>
  summarise(
    observations =
      n(),

    first_year =
      min(
        year,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    last_year =
      max(
        year,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(
    first_year,
    ticker
  )


knitr::kable(
  annual_firm_coverage,
  col.names = c(
    "Ticker",
    "Firm-year observations",
    "First year",
    "Last year"
  ),
  caption =
    "Coverage of the annual firm-level sample"
)

```

Companies entering the dataset later have shorter historical series.
Firm-specific correlations and regressions based on these firms should
therefore be interpreted more cautiously than estimates for REOCs with
long histories.

```{r appendix-rq3-descriptive-statistics}

rq3_descriptive_statistics <- fa_rq3 |>
```

### C.4 Full Macro × Firm Fundamentals Correlation Matrix

The following matrix extends the main RQ3 discussion by comparing five
macroeconomic variables with four firm-level financial characteristics.

```{r appendix-rq3-correlation-matrix}

cor_data <- fa_rq3 |>
  select(
    short_rate,
    confederation_10y,
    gdp_growth,
    sfso_inflation_according_to_the_national_consumer_price_index,
    jobless_rate_sa,
    debt_to_assets,
    net_debt_ebitda,
    roa,
    asset_growth
  )


macro_vars <- c(
  "short_rate",
  "confederation_10y",
  "gdp_growth",
  "sfso_inflation_according_to_the_national_consumer_price_index",
  "jobless_rate_sa"
)


firm_vars <- c(
  "debt_to_assets",
  "net_debt_ebitda",
  "roa",
  "asset_growth"
)


cor_matrix <- cor(
  cor_data,
  use =
    "pairwise.complete.obs",
  method =
    "pearson"
)


macro_firm_cor <- cor_matrix[
  macro_vars,
  firm_vars,
  drop = FALSE
]


macro_firm_cor_table <- as.data.frame(
  macro_firm_cor
) |>
  rownames_to_column(
    "Macroeconomic variable"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    `Macroeconomic variable` =
      recode(
        `Macroeconomic variable`,
        short_rate =
          "Short-term rate",
        confederation_10y =
          "10Y government yield",
        gdp_growth =
          "GDP growth",
        sfso_inflation_according_to_the_national_consumer_price_index =
          "Inflation",
        jobless_rate_sa =
          "Unemployment"
      )
  ) |>
  rename(
    `Debt / Assets` =
      debt_to_assets,
    `Net Debt / EBITDA` =
      net_debt_ebitda,
    ROA =
      roa,
    `Asset Growth` =
      asset_growth
  ) |>
  mutate(
    across(
      where(is.numeric),
      ~ round(.x, 2)
    )
  )


knitr::kable(
  macro_firm_cor_table,
  caption =
    "Pearson correlations between macroeconomic indicators and firm fundamentals"
)

```

The correlation matrix confirms that most macro-fundamental
relationships are relatively weak. The most notable pooled relationship
is between the 10-year government yield and debt-to-assets.

```{r appendix-rq3-correlation-heatmap, fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
          correlation
        )
    )
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    midpoint = 0,
    limits = c(
      -1,
      1
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Macroeconomic Conditions and REOC Fundamentals",
    subtitle = "Pearson correlation matrix",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    fill = "Correlation"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid =
      element_blank(),
    axis.text.x =
      element_text(
        angle = 30,
        hjust = 1
      )
  )

```

Positive values indicate that the variables tend to move in the same
direction, while negative values indicate opposite co-movement. Values
close to zero indicate little linear association.

### C.6 Full Firm-Specific Yield–Leverage Correlation Table

The main report visualises the heterogeneous relationship between the
10-year Confederation yield and leverage. The complete numerical results
are reported below.

```{r appendix-rq3-yield-leverage-table}

firm_yield_correlations <- fa_rq3 |>
  group_by(ticker) |>
  summarise(
    observations =
      sum(
        complete.cases(
          confederation_10y,
          debt_to_assets
        )
      ),

    correlation =
      cor(
        confederation_10y,
        debt_to_assets,
        use =
          "complete.obs"
      ),

    .groups =
      "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(
    desc(
      correlation
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    correlation =
      round(
        correlation,
        3
      )
  )


knitr::kable(
  firm_yield_correlations,
  col.names = c(
    "Ticker",
    "Observations",
    "Correlation"
  ),
  caption =
    "Firm-specific correlations between the 10-year Confederation yield and debt-to-assets"
)

```

The full table demonstrates that the pooled positive correlation masks
considerable heterogeneity across firms. Firms with shorter histories
should be interpreted cautiously because their correlations are based on
substantially fewer annual observations.

### C.7 Short-Term Interest Rates and Leverage

The main report focuses on the long-term government yield because it
produced the strongest pooled relationship with debt-to-assets. For
completeness, the short-term interest-rate relationship is also
reported.

```{r appendix-rq3-short-rate-leverage, fig.width=9, fig.height=6}

short_rate_leverage_corr <- fa_rq3 |>
  summarise(
    correlation =
      cor(
        short_rate,
        debt_to_assets,
        use =
          "complete.obs"
      )
  )


ggplot(
  fa_rq3 |>
    filter(
      !is.na(short_rate),
      !is.na(debt_to_assets)
    ),
  aes(
    x = short_rate,
    y = debt_to_assets
  )
) +
  geom_point(
    alpha = 0.45
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = TRUE
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Short-Term Interest Rates and REOC Leverage",
    subtitle = "Annual firm-year observations",
    x = "Short-term interest rate (%)",
    y = "Debt to assets (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor =
      element_blank()
  )

```

```{r appendix-rq3-short-rate-correlation-table}

short_rate_change_corr <- fa_rq3 |>
  summarise(
    `Rate level vs. leverage level` =
      cor(
        short_rate,
        debt_to_assets,
        use =
          "complete.obs"
      ),

    `Rate change vs. leverage change` =
      cor(
        delta_short_rate,
        delta_debt_to_assets,
        use =
          "complete.obs"
      )
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to =
      "Relationship",
    values_to =
      "Correlation"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Correlation =
      round(
        Correlation,
        3
      )
  )


knitr::kable(
  short_rate_change_corr,
  caption =
    "Short-term interest rates and leverage: levels and annual changes"
)

```

The short-rate results are weaker than the long-term yield relationship
and therefore remain supplementary to the main RQ3 analysis.

### C.8 Firm Size and Leverage

Firm size may itself be associated with capital structure. The following
analysis compares total assets with debt-to-assets.

```{r appendix-rq3-size-leverage, fig.width=9, fig.height=6}

size_leverage_correlation <- fa_rq3 |>
  summarise(
    correlation =
      cor(
        fa_total_assets,
        debt_to_assets,
        use =
          "complete.obs"
      )
  )


ggplot(
  fa_rq3 |>
    filter(
      !is.na(fa_total_assets),
      !is.na(debt_to_assets)
    ),
  aes(
    x = fa_total_assets,
    y = debt_to_assets
  )
) +
  geom_point(
    alpha = 0.45,
    size = 2
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = TRUE
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels =
      scales::label_number(
        big.mark = "'"
      )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Firm Size and REOC Leverage",
    subtitle = "Annual firm-year observations",
    x = "Total assets",
    y = "Debt to assets (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor =
      element_blank()
  )

```

The pooled relationship between total assets and leverage is weak. Firm
size alone therefore does not appear to explain much of the
cross-sectional variation in debt-to-assets within the sample.
